authoritative_sources.title: Guidelines to the Practice of Anesthesia—Revised Edition 2026
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: The CAS guideline page identifies the 2026 revised edition as current; the document states that it is updated annually and supersedes all previous editions.

supported_recommendations.statement: Preanesthetic assessment should document relevant medical and surgical history, current and recent drug therapy, prior and family anesthetic reactions, focused physical findings, relevant investigations, and an ASA Physical Status classification so that anesthetic management can be planned.

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Routine laboratory blood testing, ECG, and chest radiography are not recommended for asymptomatic patients having low-risk surgery; tests should be ordered only when the result could change perioperative management.

evidence_boundaries.statement: ASA Physical Status is one documented component of preanesthetic assessment; it does not replace the history, physical examination, procedure-specific assessment, or selectively indicated investigations.

evidence_notes: Evidence extraction is limited to the diagnostic structure of adult preoperative assessment, selective testing, and ASA classification required by SU-A-03.

source_citations.locator: Section 4, The Preanesthetic Period, and Section 4.1, Preoperative Testing

authoritative_sources.title: Guidelines to the Practice of Anesthesia—Revised Edition 2026
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: The CAS guideline page identifies the 2026 revised edition as current; the document states that it is updated annually and supersedes all previous editions.

supported_recommendations.statement: Preoperative cardiopulmonary and aspiration-risk assessment should integrate the patient's comorbidities, current drug therapy, proposed procedure, and urgency; investigations are targeted to findings that could change perioperative management, and urgent cases require an explicit balance between delay and aspiration risk.

source_citations.locator: Section 4; Section 4.1 table of preoperative tests; Section 4.2 Fasting Guidelines, pp. 12–14

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: A single comorbidity or abnormal test does not determine operative suitability in isolation; testing and planning remain patient-, medication-, and procedure-specific.

evidence_boundaries.statement: For an urgent procedure, fasting status is not an automatic cancellation rule; the risk of delaying the procedure must be weighed against the risk of aspiration.

evidence_notes: Evidence extraction is restricted to recognition and preoperative risk stratification for cardiopulmonary comorbidity and aspiration risk in SU-A-05; it does not encode a treatment algorithm.

authoritative_sources.title: Guidelines to the Practice of Anesthesia—Revised Edition 2026
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: The 2026 CAS edition is the current annual revision and expressly supersedes earlier editions.

supported_recommendations.statement: During general anesthesia lasting at least 30 minutes, monitor core temperature continuously and recognize deviation from the usual 36–37 °C target as requiring assessment and correction unless hypothermia is specifically indicated by the patient or procedure.

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: For neuraxial anesthesia lasting at least 30 minutes, continuous or intermittent temperature monitoring is recommended rather than the continuous-core-monitoring requirement used for general anesthesia.

evidence_boundaries.statement: The 36–37 °C target applies when there is no surgical or patient indication for intraoperative hypothermia.

evidence_notes: Evidence extraction is limited to recognition and monitoring of perioperative temperature deviation for SU-A-13.

authoritative_sources.title: Anesthesia advanced circulatory life support
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia / Canadian Anesthesiologists' Society
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: The stable diagnostic physiology and perioperative shock-differential content is used with the current 2026 CAS monitoring standard; no newer CAS replacement addressing this diagnostic scope was found.

supported_recommendations.statement: Recognize intraoperative hypotension through required blood-pressure and perioperative perfusion monitoring, verify the signal and trend, and evaluate likely physiology rather than assuming hypovolemia; causes include loss of preload and obstructive or right-ventricular shock states that may not respond safely to indiscriminate fluid.

source_citations.locator: Hypovolemia and systolic and pulse pressure variation; severe hypotension discussion

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Respiratory variation in arterial pressure can be misleading in right-ventricular and obstructive shock, including tamponade, tension pneumothorax, auto-PEEP, and pulmonary hypertension.

source_citations.locator: Hypovolemia and systolic and pulse pressure variation

evidence_boundaries.statement: A blood-pressure value alone does not identify shock mechanism; integrate oxygenation, perfusion, rhythm, ventilation, surgical context, and response to a cautious intervention.

evidence_notes: Evidence extraction is limited to diagnostic recognition and etiologic differentiation of intraoperative hypotension/shock for SU-A-15.

authoritative_sources.title: Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Current live CAS CPD module at retrieval, explicitly covering risk factors and typical and atypical LAST recognition.

authoritative_sources.title: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Peer-reviewed Canadian clinical review with stable recognition features, used alongside the current CAS LAST module and 2026 CAS practice guideline.

supported_recommendations.statement: Suspect local anesthetic systemic toxicity when oral numbness, metallic taste, dizziness, drowsiness, or disorientation occurs soon after local-anesthetic administration; severe or delayed toxicity can present with seizures, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, or isolated cardiovascular disturbance.

source_citations.locator: Module objectives: recognize typical and atypical clinical features
Signs and symptoms and severe manifestations sections

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Do not exclude LAST because early neurologic prodromes are absent or because the presentation is delayed; severe manifestations may occur hours after initial symptoms.

source_citations.locator: Module objective 3, typical and atypical clinical features
Severe manifestations may appear up to 6 hours after initial symptom onset

evidence_boundaries.statement: Temporal association with local-anesthetic exposure and compatible neurologic or cardiovascular findings supports the diagnosis, but competing causes of seizure, hypoxia, hypotension, and arrhythmia must still be considered while emergency treatment proceeds.

source_citations.locator: Signs, symptoms, and severe manifestations sections

evidence_notes: Evidence extraction is restricted to clinical recognition and diagnostic boundaries for LAST in SU-A-25; treatment dosing is outside this packet's DIAGNOSIS requirement.

source_citations.locator: Five things to know about LAST

authoritative_sources.title: Common side effects after anesthesia
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Live CAS educational page at retrieval; stable descriptions of common postanesthetic effects are paired with the superseding 2026 CAS PACU monitoring standard.

supported_recommendations.statement: In the immediate postoperative period, recognize pain and postoperative nausea/vomiting as common anesthetic complications while simultaneously assessing consciousness, heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and respiratory rate for more urgent airway, ventilatory, or circulatory complications.

source_citations.locator: Sections 5.8 and 6.1, PACU assessment and monitoring, pp. 17–18
Nausea and vomiting after surgery and other common side effects

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Do not attribute reduced consciousness, hypoxemia, apnea, hypotension, or bradycardia to uncomplicated nausea or pain; these findings require immediate assessment and monitoring in the PACU.

evidence_boundaries.statement: Common postoperative symptoms remain diagnoses of exclusion when vital signs, oxygenation, ventilation, or consciousness are abnormal; PACU discharge requires a validated assessment and facility criteria.

evidence_notes: Evidence extraction is limited to recognition and triage of common immediate postanesthetic complications in SU-A-27; medication selection and dosing are not encoded.

authoritative_sources.title: Chronic Pain in Canada: Laying a Foundation for Action
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Health Canada, Canadian Pain Task Force
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Health Canada's current chronic-pain pages continue to link the three Canadian Pain Task Force reports; this first report contains the diagnostic mechanism and classification evidence required here.

supported_recommendations.statement: Diagnose chronic primary pain when pain persists or recurs for more than three months, is associated with significant emotional distress or functional disability, and is not better accounted for by another diagnosis; sensitization-related nociplastic pain reflects altered sensory-neuron responsiveness rather than direct tissue or nerve damage.

source_citations.locator: Section 1, biological mechanisms of pain and Chronic pain is a disease in its own right

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Chronic secondary pain begins as a symptom of an underlying condition and may persist after that condition is treated; it should not be relabelled chronic primary pain when another diagnosis better accounts for it.

source_citations.locator: Section 1, chronic primary and chronic secondary pain classification

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: The national Health Canada expert task-force report directly defines chronic primary, chronic secondary, neuropathic, nociceptive, and sensitization-related nociplastic pain; no current Canadian specialty-society guideline covering this complete diagnostic scope was found.

evidence_boundaries.statement: Structural imaging may not identify a meaningful cause of chronic primary pain; assess functional and emotional impact and exclude treatable secondary causes without assuming that absent structural findings make the pain unreal.

source_citations.locator: Section 2, Recognition that pain is real and multi-dimensional will support improved diagnosis

evidence_notes: Evidence extraction is limited to diagnostic definitions and sensitization mechanisms for chronic pain in SU-A-30.

source_citations.locator: Sections 1–2, diagnostic mechanisms and chronic-pain classification

authoritative_sources.title: Updated Guide for the Management of Malignant Hyperthermia
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Current live CAS CPD module at retrieval, explicitly addressing prompt recognition, differential diagnosis, dantrolene treatment, post-crisis observation, and referral.

supported_recommendations.statement: Suspect malignant hyperthermia when an anesthetized patient develops otherwise unexplained signs of a hypermetabolic reaction; rapidly evaluate plausible alternatives while initiating prompt crisis treatment, including dantrolene, because delay increases the risk of renal failure, cardiac dysfunction, coagulopathy, and death.

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Malignant-hyperthermia findings are nonspecific; alternative diagnoses should be assessed rapidly, but diagnostic uncertainty must not postpone treatment of a suspected crisis.

source_citations.locator: Module overview: nonspecific hypermetabolic signs and rapid rejection of alternative diagnoses

evidence_boundaries.statement: After an apparent crisis resolves, observe for at least 24 hours because recrudescence can occur, and refer survivors and family members to a specialized malignant-hyperthermia centre for testing and counselling.

evidence_notes: Evidence extraction is restricted to recognition, immediate diagnostic boundary, and post-crisis verification for malignant hyperthermia in SU-A-33; no detailed dosing algorithm is encoded.

authoritative_sources.title: QUELICIN (Succinylcholine Chloride Injection USP) Prescribing Information
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Pfizer Canada ULC; reviewed through Health Canada Drug Product Database
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Health Canada's current Drug Product Database lists QUELICIN as marketed and links this February 26, 2024 monograph.

supported_recommendations.statement: Suspect reduced plasma pseudocholinesterase activity when neuromuscular blockade and apnea persist unexpectedly after succinylcholine; the drug is normally hydrolyzed by plasma cholinesterase, and reduced activity increases the likelihood of prolonged blockade requiring continued ventilatory support.

source_citations.locator: Action and Clinical Pharmacology; Warnings; Precautions—Reduced Plasma Cholinesterase Activity, pp. 2, 4, and 6

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Distinguish pseudocholinesterase-related prolonged Phase I block from Phase II block after large or repeated succinylcholine doses; anticholinesterase drugs given before succinylcholine is metabolized can prolong rather than shorten paralysis.

source_citations.locator: Action and Clinical Pharmacology and Precautions—Phase II block, pp. 2 and 5

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: The current Health Canada-linked product monograph directly supports the pharmacologic mechanism, diagnostic distinction, and ventilatory safety boundary; no current CAS guideline devoted to pseudocholinesterase deficiency was found.

evidence_boundaries.statement: Prolonged postoperative paralysis is not diagnostic of inherited pseudocholinesterase deficiency by itself; large/repeated dosing, Phase II block, acquired reductions in enzyme activity, and interacting drugs must be considered.

source_citations.locator: Precautions—Phase II block, Reduced Plasma Cholinesterase Activity, and Drug Interactions, pp. 5–7

evidence_notes: Evidence extraction is restricted to recognition and differentiation of prolonged succinylcholine blockade for SU-A-34.

source_citations.locator: Action and Clinical Pharmacology; Warnings; Precautions

authoritative_sources.title: Canadian Cardiovascular Society Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Stable Ischemic Heart Disease
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: The current CCS guideline library still lists this stable-ischemic-heart-disease diagnosis guideline; the CCS development page identifies a new acute ischemic heart disease guideline as in development for 2028, not as a superseding publication.

supported_recommendations.statement: Assess stable chest pain by symptom characteristics and pretest likelihood: typical angina is substernal discomfort with characteristic quality and duration, provoked by exertion or emotional stress, and relieved promptly by rest or nitroglycerin; select further testing according to risk and the clinical question.

source_citations.locator: Section I and Figure 2, chest-pain criteria and diagnostic pathway, pp. 839–841

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Chest pain is not synonymous with coronary ischemia; urgent cardiovascular, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, chest-wall, neurologic, and psychiatric alternatives must be considered from the presentation.

source_citations.locator: Table 2, Alternative diagnoses to angina for patients with chest pain, p. 840

evidence_boundaries.statement: The stable-ischemic-heart-disease pathway does not replace emergency evaluation of an acute or unstable chest-pain syndrome; high-risk features require an urgent pathway rather than routine outpatient stress testing.

evidence_notes: Evidence extraction is limited to the cardiac differential and diagnostic framing of chest pain for SU-C-03; acute treatment algorithms are outside this packet.
